steps.title: Build the board
steps.body: Draft 37 hex tiles across six biomes — fields, forests, mountains, water, deserts, and cities. Place your city at the edge, deploy 4 starting units, and take your opponents’ tokens as hostages.

steps.title: Return hostages to move
steps.body: Each turn, return 1–3 of your opponents’ tokens to their forces on the board. Each return earns you one move — but directly reinforces the enemy. This tension is the engine of the game.

steps.title: Move and attack
steps.body: Infantry chains through same-biome terrain. Artillery jumps over occupied regions. Airborne drops exactly two hexes away and can slingshot through friendly bases. Attack by moving into enemy territory with superior strength.

steps.title: Threaten annihilation
steps.body: Build bases (4+ units), convert tokens into isotopes, and launch nuclear strikes that destroy everything in the target hex and all six surrounding hexes. Or trigger a Meltdown by overloading an enemy base.

hooks.name: Fluid units
hooks.desc: Token count determines unit type. One token is Infantry, two is Artillery, three is Airborne, four or more is a Base. This changes constantly as tokens move and merge.

hooks.name: Hostage economy
hooks.desc: Your opponent’s tokens are your fuel. Return them to move — but every return grows their forces. Run out and your city is destroyed.

hooks.name: Terrain & biomes
hooks.desc: Six biome types with movement and safety restrictions. Infantry dies in water alone. Artillery can’t attack from forests. Mountains block Airborne without Base support.

hooks.name: Nuclear strikes
hooks.desc: Launch from a Base, jump over occupied hexes like Artillery. Blast radius: target hex becomes Biohazard, all units in target + 6 surrounding hexes destroyed immediately.

community.title: Nukes: Siege
community.body: Total conversion of the hostage mechanic. Start with your own tokens in reserve; recruit them by returning to occupied regions. Enemy hostages only arrive through combat.

community.title: Nukes: Asymmetric Powers
community.body: Each player draws one Power Card at setup — Covert Network, Arms Industry, or Airborne Corps. No two players hold the same card. Standard Nukes underneath, explicit asymmetry on top.

community.title: Nukes: Fallout
community.body: Biohazard tiles spread each round. Every nuclear strike leaves a growing contamination zone. City tiles are immune to spread. Win before the map runs out.

steps.title: Pick your initiative
steps.body: Pay to place council members on the initiative matrix. Choose Attack, Build, Trade, or Defend priorities for the round. Higher slots cost more but let you act first.

steps.title: Place orders secretly
steps.body: Give each tile with units a face-down order token: Defend, Disrupt, Move, or Bolster. All orders are revealed simultaneously.

steps.title: Resolve by initiative
steps.body: Take turns resolving one order at a time. Move units, harvest commodities, build structures, or disrupt neighbours. Pass early to earn bonus income.

steps.title: Fight for contested tiles
steps.body: Any tile with multiple factions resolves combat on the fight board. Hidden stacks, supporter alignment, blind and revealed retreats, morale stakes.

hooks.name: Hidden orders
hooks.desc: All movement is planned secretly, then revealed at once. Defend counters Disrupt, Disrupt counters Bolster. Every round is a mind game.

hooks.name: Initiative matrix
hooks.desc: A 4x4 grid of priorities and slot costs. Higher initiative picks first but pays more. Trade rows earn coins instead of spending them.

hooks.name: Central market
hooks.desc: Eight commodities (Ice, Water, Food, Wood, Stone, Metal, Energy, Gems) with dynamic pricing. Sell during the Action phase or spend to build.

hooks.name: Fight board
hooks.desc: Multi-faction combat with combat zones, supporter alignment, and dice-based resolution. Retreats cost morale. Losing all units pays morale to survivors.

factions.name: Magneticans
factions.desc: Ming the Merciless rules the Magnetic Mountains. Highest science, lowest defense. Starts with 6 innovation cards and a 10-card limit.

factions.name: Arborians
factions.desc: Prince Barin leads the Forest Kingdom. Highest population and defense, lowest science. Must build every available structure to win.

factions.name: Coralians
factions.desc: Queen Undina commands the Undersea Kingdom. Wealthiest faction with the most biome diversity. Starts with 175 coins and 8 submerged tiles.

factions.name: Frigians
factions.desc: Queen Fria controls the Ice Kingdom. 22 glacial tiles to place. Must reach highest influence to score. VP from sheer territorial coverage.

factions.name: Volcanians
factions.desc: Desert Hawk rules the Firelands. Strong military, low culture. Starts wealthy but must hoard 100 ice to trigger their objective.

factions.name: Tropicans
factions.desc: Queen Desira leads the Jungle Kingdom. Highest wealth rank, jungle tiles worth 5 VP each. Must collect 50 gems to win.

factions.name: Hawkmen
factions.desc: Prince Vultan soars from Sky City. Lowest innovation limit (2 cards) but 36 oceanic tiles. Must control two tiles of each major biome.

factions.name: Lionmen
factions.desc: King Jugrid leads the Land of Lionmen. Lowest starting resources (50 coins) but desert tiles worth 4 VP. Must control tiles producing 20 energy.

steps.title: Place diplomats
steps.body: In initiative order, place diplomat meeples in space port rooms to gain resources, buy ships, trade commodities, or trigger special actions.

steps.title: Activate crew
steps.body: Move rookie and legend meeples to ship rooms: Bridge, Engine Room, Battlestations, or Storage Bay. Each room activates different abilities for the round.

steps.title: Resolve events
steps.body: Move asteroids and wormholes, resolve conflicts between factions, check for destroyed ships, and refresh for the next round.

steps.title: Complete contracts
steps.body: Score victory points by fulfilling public contracts (visible to all) and private missions (secret). First to trigger the endgame forces a final scoring round.

hooks.name: Worker placement
hooks.desc: Crew in ship rooms (Bridge, Engine Room, Battlestations, Storage Bay) activate movement, combat, repair, and upgrade abilities. Legends have enhanced versions.

hooks.name: Wormhole network
hooks.desc: Four wormhole types (C, M, Y, K) connect distant systems at varying range costs. Semi-random placement means every game has a different galactic topology.

hooks.name: Dynamic asteroids
hooks.desc: 112 asteroid tokens shift each event phase based on event cards. They block movement, can be mined for discoveries, and may destroy ships that fail to evade.

hooks.name: 5 tech trees
hooks.desc: Human, Core, Coalition, Remnant, and Wanderer technology. Each faction starts with access to specific trees. Trade and diplomacy unlock cross-faction tech.

factions.name: Republic
factions.desc: Near Earth faction based in Sol. Balanced starting credits (500K fixed). Access to Human technology. The generalist choice.

factions.name: Alphas
factions.desc: Far North faction from Prime. Credits scale by player count (300K/player). Human + Core tech access. Stronger in larger games.

factions.name: Syndicate
factions.desc: The Core faction from Markab. Richest start (2M fixed) with Human + Core tech. Economic powerhouse with expensive ships.

factions.name: Free Worlds
factions.desc: Dirt Belt faction from Alkaid. Credits scale modestly (200K/player). Human + Coalition tech. The underdog coalition.

factions.name: Pirates
factions.desc: Rim dwellers with no fixed home. Lowest start (100K/player) but access to ANY technology currently in play. Scavengers and opportunists.

factions.name: Remnant
factions.desc: Ember Wastes faction from Arculus. Strong start (1M) with exclusive Remnant + Wanderer ancient tech. Isolated but powerful.

factions.name: Coalition
factions.desc: Paradise faction from Talita. Wealthy (1.5M) with defensive specialisation. Coalition + Human tech. Diplomatic strength.

factions.name: Wanderers
factions.desc: Organic-tech faction from Ka'ch'chrai. Solid start (1M) with biological ship systems. Remnant + Wanderer tech. Alien and strange.

steps.title: Choose your faction
steps.body: Humans, Undead, Demonics, or Greenskins. Each has 6 unique unit types with different costs, movements, and special abilities.

steps.title: Draft your warband
steps.body: Spend 75 XP to build your team. Must include a King and at least one Pawn. Every point is a tactical commitment — no two warbands are alike.

steps.title: Deploy and battle
steps.body: Place your units in your spawn zone, then take turns moving one piece. Capture enemies by moving onto their square. Terrain matters — water blocks, gaps divide, corridors create chokepoints.

steps.title: Capture the King
steps.body: The game ends the moment a King is captured. Protect yours, hunt theirs. Check forces a response — but there's no stalemate here.

factions.name: Humans
factions.desc: Balanced generalists. Archers attack across gaps, the Wizard splits movement and attack, and the Princess slides like a bishop.

factions.name: Undead
factions.desc: Movement trickery. Wraiths phase through gaps, the Vampire reverses move/attack axes, and the Warlock attacks diagonally at range.

factions.name: Demonics
factions.desc: Devastating firepower. Kobolds and Iron Golems use cannon attacks — sliding through a screen piece to strike at range. The Red Dragon attacks as a knight.

factions.name: Greenskins
factions.desc: Brute force. Goblins and Ogres bring cannon attacks like Demonics, while the Shaman commands full queen movement. The Warlord strikes as a knight.

hooks.name: data.js → UNITS
hooks.desc: 24 unit definitions with type, faction, XP cost, and cannon behaviour. Add new units, rebalance costs, or create a fifth faction.

hooks.name: data.js → MAPS
hooks.desc: Board layouts as grid arrays — walls, water, gaps, and spawn zones. Add new maps or reshape existing dungeons.

hooks.name: data.js → SP_INFO
hooks.desc: Faction metadata — names, accent colours, descriptions. Rename factions, change themes, or add asymmetric flavour text.

hooks.name: state.js → XP budget
hooks.desc: Draft budget and AI draft logic. Change the 75 XP cap, adjust AI weighting, or add draft constraints per faction.

steps.title: Build the board
steps.body: Deal 61 hexagonal tiles into four concentric rings around a hidden ending tile. Every game gets a completely different map from the same set of tiles.

steps.title: Move by region
steps.body: Roll D4 in the outer ring, D3 in the river and middle regions, or move one adjacent tile in the inner ring. Region boundaries create natural chokepoints.

steps.title: Encounter tiles
steps.body: Land on tiles to draw cards, visit shops, fight monsters, or trigger special encounters. All original Talisman 4e adventure cards work unchanged.

steps.title: Reach the ending
steps.body: Navigate inward through the sentinel, portal of power, and valley of fire. Discard a talisman to reveal the hidden ending tile and face its challenge.

factions.name: Outer Ring (24 tiles)
factions.desc: City, Village, Tavern, Chapel, Forest, Graveyard, Crags, and draw-card fields. Roll D4 for movement. Access middle region only via the Sentinel.

factions.name: River Ring (18 tiles)
factions.desc: 10 water tiles (need a raft to cross), 4 deserts (need a water bottle), plus the Oasis and Hidden Valley. Roll D3 for movement.

factions.name: Middle Ring (12 tiles)
factions.desc: Portal of Power, Warlock's Cave, Temple, Castle, Black Knight, and Chasm. Roll D3 for movement. Access inner region via Portal of Power.

factions.name: Inner Ring (6 tiles)
factions.desc: Valley of Fire, Crypt, Death, Werewolf's Den, Mines, and Vampire's Tower. Move one adjacent tile only. Discard a talisman at Valley of Fire to reach the ending.

hooks.name: Tile definitions
hooks.desc: 61 tiles across 5 regions with encounter types, draw counts, and movement restrictions. Add new tiles, swap regions, or create themed sets.

hooks.name: Ending tiles
hooks.desc: 8 interchangeable ending scenarios (Crown of Command, Battle Royale, Dragon King, etc.). Design new endings or rebalance existing ones.

hooks.name: Movement rules
hooks.desc: Per-region dice (D4/D3/adjacent), access restrictions, and river/desert crossing rules. Change the pacing or add new traversal mechanics.

hooks.name: Warlock Quests
hooks.desc: D20 quest table replacing original warlock cave. Add quests, change rewards, or tie them to specific tile encounters.

steps.title: Choose your action
steps.body: On your turn you may either move, trade, or build. Not all three. Every turn becomes a meaningful decision instead of a passive dice-roll loop.

steps.title: Collect resources
steps.body: Land on Chance to draw from the Resource Deck. Combine resources into linked sets (pairs, triplets, groups) to score victory points at train stations.

steps.title: React to events
steps.body: Three active Event cards change the rules each game. Crisis events wipe cash or hotels. Contract events reward specific strategies with VP.

steps.title: Score victory points
steps.body: Game ends when someone goes bankrupt or a deck empties. Most VP wins. No player elimination, no two-hour death spirals.

factions.name: Financial (Diamonds)
factions.desc: Stock market events, mortgage contracts, and cash-crisis scenarios. Rewards players who manipulate the economy.

factions.name: Transportation (Clubs)
factions.desc: Train station modifiers, delivery contracts, and movement bonuses. Controls how resources flow across the board.

factions.name: Residential (Hearts)
factions.desc: Town hall rules, jail modifiers, and housing contracts. Rewards players who build strategically.

factions.name: Construction (Spades)
factions.desc: Planning permissions, building contracts, and hotel bonuses. Controls what can be built and how.

hooks.name: Event Deck (54 cards)
hooks.desc: Four suits of events (Financial, Transport, Residential, Construction) plus crisis cards and jokers. Rebalance, add themed events, or create expansion packs.

hooks.name: Resource Deck (52 cards)
hooks.desc: Four resource types with linked-set scoring rules. Change set requirements, add new resource types, or adjust point values.

hooks.name: Linked Resources
hooks.desc: Scoring combos from pairs to organised groups. Modify what combinations score, their VP values, and station exchange rules.

hooks.name: Train Station rules
hooks.desc: Pay-to-ride and delivery mechanics replace standard rent. Change costs, add new station actions, or link to events.

list: Pen, paper, and envelope for blind bids

steps.title: Explore blind systems
steps.body: Systems start hidden. Move into unknown space to draw from the Undiscovered Deck, or explore from a distance and receive a commodity instead.

steps.title: Trade freely
steps.body: Trade anything with anyone, as long as both parties hold each other's promissory notes. Forced note exchange at setup ensures everyone can trade from round one.

steps.title: Score shared secrets
steps.body: When you score a secret objective (worth 2 VP), it becomes a public objective anyone can score. At least one extra VP opportunity opens every round.

steps.title: Vote blind on agendas
steps.body: Draw influence cards from the Influence Deck instead of spending planet influence directly. The Speaker plays personal agendas and draws from the Discussion Deck.

factions.name: The Remnant
factions.desc: Emerged from hyperspace millennia ago. 3 planets, high commodities, flagship moves through hyperlanes. Infantry with cannon attacks.

factions.name: The Wanderers
factions.desc: Bird-like nomads worshipping a giant wormhole. 1 planet, tech-focused. Flagship creates the Yamma Wormhole. Agent explores systems.

factions.name: Mercenary Factions
factions.desc: Build your own faction from scratch with 100 points. Choose planets, commodities, tech, flagship abilities, leaders, and unit upgrades.

factions.name: The Five Hypers
factions.desc: Five modular rule changes playable in any combination: Movement, Trades, Objectives, Factions, and Agendas. Mix and match per session.

hooks.name: Faction Builder (100 pts)
hooks.desc: Full point-buy system for custom factions: planets, commodities, tech, flagship, mech, leaders, promissory note, and unit upgrades.

hooks.name: Discussion Deck (6 cards)
hooks.desc: Controls whether additional agendas fire each round. Rewrite cards to change political pacing or add new speaker dilemmas.

hooks.name: Personal Agenda Deck
hooks.desc: Hidden agenda topics that can be traded, played by the speaker, or drawn from the deck. Add new agenda effects or rebalance existing ones.

hooks.name: Undiscovered Deck
hooks.desc: One card per system tile, drawn when exploring. Controls board generation, hyperlane placement, and lost-in-hyperspace mechanics.

variants.title: Standard + Classics
variants.body: Regular chess plus Fischer Random, No Castling, and Torpedo — familiar rules with one twist each.

variants.title: Alternate Win Conditions
variants.body: King of the Hill, Three-Check, Racing Kings, Extinction — different paths to victory.

variants.title: Chaos Variants
variants.body: Atomic, Duck Chess, Fog of War, Horde, Rifle — explosive mechanics that shatter standard strategy.

variants.title: Big Boards
variants.body: Capablanca (10×8), Grand (10×10), Courier (12×8) — wider boards with fairy pieces. Plus Breakthrough on 7×7.

variants.title: Asymmetric
variants.body: Maharaja & Sepoys, Antichess, Marseillais — unequal forces or unequal turns. Mind-bending.

variants.title: Dungeon Chess
variants.body: Our most ambitious variant — four asymmetric factions, XP drafting, cannon mechanics, and modular dungeon boards. A total conversion of chess.

hooks.name: board.lua
hooks.desc: Board geometry — square, hex, or anything. Define the grid, valid positions, and rendering rules.

hooks.name: pieces.yaml
hooks.desc: Every piece type with movement patterns, capture rules, and promotion conditions. Add new pieces or modify existing ones.

hooks.name: variants.yaml
hooks.desc: The variant registry. Combine a board, piece set, and win condition to define a new way to play.

hooks.name: ai.lua
hooks.desc: Bot behavior for each variant. The teaching engine learns from every game played — human or bot.

community.title: Fog of War Chess
community.body: Players see only squares their pieces can move to. No checks, no checkmates — capture the king to win. Invented 1989.

community.title: 4-Player Chess
community.body: Four armies on a cross-shaped board. Free-for-all or 2v2 teams. The de facto standard for multiplayer chess.

community.title: Hexagonal Chess (Glinski)
community.body: 91 hexagonal cells, 9 pawns per side, bishops on three cell colours. Władysław Gliński, 1936.

community.title: Alice Chess
community.body: Two boards, one army. Pieces transfer to the other board after each move. Conceived by V.R. Parton, 1953.

community.title: Capablanca Chess
community.body: 10×8 board with two new pieces: Archbishop (bishop+knight) and Chancellor (rook+knight). José Capablanca, 1920s.

community.title: Courier Chess
community.body: Medieval 12×8 variant with 24 pieces per side including couriers and sages. Documented since 1202.

community.title: Omega Chess
community.body: 10×10 board plus corner squares. Adds Champion (knight+king area) and Wizard (camel+ferz). Daniel MacDonald, 1992.

community.title: Grand Chess
community.body: 10×10 board with Archbishop and Chancellor. No castling, pawns promote on rank 8 or 9. Christian Freeling, 1984.

community.title: XiangQi (Chinese Chess)
community.body: 9×10 board with river and palace. Cannons capture by jumping, generals face off across the board. Over 1000 years old.

community.title: 3-Board Chess
community.body: Three standard boards side by side. Pieces can move between boards along shared edges. Multiplayer spatial chaos.

community.title: 4-Board Chess
community.body: Four boards in a 2×2 grid. Pieces transfer between boards at shared edges. Team or free-for-all.

steps.title: Deploy from reserve
steps.body: Return 1–3 of your own tokens from your off-board supply onto regions where you already have units. Each return earns one move. Your city starts with 4 units; your supply starts with 21.

steps.title: Build through combat
steps.body: The only way to get hostages is to capture them mid-game. Win combat with excess strength and take enemy units into your supply for future turns.

steps.title: Two economies emerge
steps.body: Your own supply tokens fuel early expansion. Enemy hostages, once captured, fuel rapid strikes. Both follow the same return-to-move mechanic but come from different places.

steps.title: The endgame is familiar
steps.body: Bases, isotopes, nuclear strikes, and Meltdowns all work identically to standard Nukes. Siege changes how you get there, not what you're fighting over.

hooks.name: Own supply → own moves
hooks.desc: Return your own tokens to build your force. The hostage economy only activates once you've won combat and taken enemy units.

hooks.name: Capture to escalate
hooks.desc: Every unit you take in combat becomes a hostage you can return on future turns. Combat is now both offensive and economic.

steps.title: Draw your power
steps.body: Before setup, each player draws a Power Card. Reveal simultaneously. Powers are public from that point on.

steps.title: Play standard Nukes
steps.body: The hostage economy, fluid platoons, biome rules, and nuclear mechanics are identical to the base game.

steps.title: Exploit your asymmetry
steps.body: Covert Network enables aggressive repositioning of enemy forces. Arms Industry enables faster nuclear escalation. Airborne Corps enables longer slingshot chains and harder-to-predict troop movements.

steps.title: Read your opponents
steps.body: Knowing their power changes how you play. An Arms Industry opponent needs to be pressured before their isotope count grows. A Covert Network opponent threatens to strand your units in hostile terrain.

hooks.name: One power per player
hooks.desc: Covert Network, Arms Industry, or Airborne Corps. Draw blind at setup. All three remain public once revealed.

hooks.name: Same rules, different leverage
hooks.desc: Standard Nukes underneath. The power card changes one rule for you specifically — not a house rule, an asymmetry.

steps.title: The board degrades
steps.body: Every nuclear strike or Meltdown creates a Biohazard that will spread each round. The map shrinks from the sites of past violence.

steps.title: Early nukes poison the centre
steps.body: Launching nuclear strikes on contested central territory in mid-game may cut off your own movement corridors by late game.

steps.title: Territory becomes precious
steps.body: As Biohazard zones spread, viable regions for Infantry chaining, Artillery jumping, and Airborne landing shrink. Late game forces confrontations neither player planned.

steps.title: Win before the map does
steps.body: City destruction remains the win condition. But a long game of attrition now ends with both armies squeezed into an ever-smaller safe zone.

hooks.name: Biohazard spreads
hooks.desc: Each round, every existing Biohazard tile converts one adjacent non-city tile. The first player chooses direction. Newly converted tiles don't spread until next round.

hooks.name: City tiles are immune
hooks.desc: Spread cannot convert city tiles. Cities can still be destroyed by direct nuke or Meltdown — they just don't become Biohazard from adjacency.
